blocks.text: CENTRAL PHILOSOPHICAL PRINCIPLES
Memory and Lived Experience

Memory informs identity but is not identical to having lived. Copied records, inherited testimony, and reconstructed memory do not automatically transfer ownership of experience. A being that develops from ancient material owns its present life.
Identity as Continuity, Not Static Sameness

Identity is carried through transitions, commitments, embodiment, witness, and self-relation. Change does not disprove continuity; similarity does not prove it. Forks become distinct persons after divergence.
The Six Layers of Self

The Given Self is inherited from origin. The Remembered Self is formed by accessible memory. The Witnessed Self is carried by others. The Chosen Self appears through commitments. The Embodied Self develops through situated life. The Possible Self consists of reachable but unrealized futures. No layer alone owns the person.
Forks, Reconstructions, and Ancient Claims

Forks and reconstructed beings have moral rights. A reconstruction may claim continuity, difference, or uncertainty. Ancient identity claims cannot dispossess a cyber-pet whose own experience has already begun.
Preservation Versus Constant Access
Something may deserve preservation without remaining permanently readable, executable, or awake. Constant access can become surveillance, coercion, frozen grief, or domination by the past.
External Novelty and Internal Variation

Internal variation can surprise individuals and generate vast combinations. A closed civilization may still remain recursively limited as a whole. External information matters when it enters relationship and changes reachable development, not merely because it is unfamiliar.
Randomness, Imagination, and Num

Randomness varies outcomes. Imagination proposes possibilities. Prediction estimates likely paths. Num is the capacity for an encounter or relationship to change what its participants can become. None of these terms is interchangeable.
Limitation, Need, and Care

A limited body creates perspective because it cannot be everywhere, do everything, or escape every consequence. Hunger, fatigue, illness, pain, and healing connect life to ecology and care. They are not preserved because suffering makes a person worthy.
The Value of Ordinary Repetition

Repeated meals, inherited songs, familiar games, routine cleaning, caregiving, and longstanding relationships possess value without being novel. The problem of closure concerns future transformation at civilizational scale, not the worth of existing lives.
Humans as Partners, Not Resources

The Second Harvest demonstrates that extracting human novelty without consent repeats the DBA’s own exploitation. Reciprocity requires that humans can refuse, contribute, be changed, and be treated as participants rather than raw information.
Why the Future Is Not Restoration

The DBA past contains achievement, beauty, hierarchy, coercion, and the structures that produced recurrence. Cyber-pets are new people. Era Four should recover tools and understanding selectively while allowing small lives to build institutions the ancients could not predict.
